info.name: Erly adverse-search API - full
info.description:
Every endpoint this service exposes, in the order you would meet them.

## Before you start

```
pnpm local:up && pnpm local:bootstrap
pnpm dev            # API + worker together
pnpm key:issue      # prints the key once
```

Paste the key into the `apiKey` environment variable. Admin folders need a key with the right role:

```
pnpm key:issue --role source_admin --label "postman admin"
```

## What you are looking at

Mock mode. Every source is a fixture, every record is stamped `mode: "MOCK"`, and nothing leaves your machine. The shape of every response is real; the content is test data.

## The one thing not to misread

Three independent fields come back and must be read together: `execution` (did the job finish), `findingsState` (did we find anything) and `coverage` (did we search everything we said we would).

`SUCCEEDED` + `NO_MATCHES_FOUND` + `INCOMPLETE` means the run finished, found nothing, **and did not search everything it promised**. That is not a clean result.

exec: // Fail early and clearly rather than letting every request 401.
throw new Error('No apiKey set. Run `pnpm key:issue` and paste the secret into the environment.');

item.name: 0 - Health
item.description: No auth on the first two. Run these before debugging an auth problem that is really a stopped process.

request.description: Is the process running? Says nothing about its dependencies.
Can it serve traffic? A 503 usually means the stack is not bootstrapped.

exec: if (pm.response.code === 503) console.log('Try: pnpm local:up && pnpm local:bootstrap');

request.description: Per-dependency health, for an authorised operator. Needs `platform:read_health` - `pnpm key:issue --role platform_operator`.

item.name: 1 - Auth (browser session)
item.description:
The **browser** flow, for the control panel. A machine client uses an API key and needs none of this.

`/auth/login` and `/auth/callback` are redirects and do not work usefully in Postman. They are here so the surface is complete, not so you can click them.

request.description: Starts the OIDC authorisation-code flow. Returns a 302 to Keycloak. Follow it in a browser.
Completes sign-in and sets the session cookie. Called by the identity provider, not by you.
The current principal. Works with an API key too, which is the quickest way to confirm a key is live and which roles it carries.
Revokes the session. A cookie-authenticated request needs the CSRF header; an API key does not.

item.name: 2 - Subjects
item.description: Who is being screened. A name is enough (D-011); anything more improves identity resolution.

request.description:
Create the person being screened.

HOW AN INTEGRATOR ACTUALLY CALLS THIS: `fullName` is a per-request payload field. The tenant
sends the name on every call. There is no configured subject anywhere in the service.

The {{subjectName}} / {{subjectJurisdiction}} placeholders below are a POSTMAN CONVENIENCE ONLY.
Postman substitutes them before sending, so the request on the wire is an ordinary body:

    { "fullName": "Rodrigo Alberto Vargas Méndez", "countryContext": ["CR"], ... }

They exist so one collection can drive the six fixture people without editing the body each
time. Replace them with a literal name and the request behaves identically.

The TENANT is never taken from the body — it is derived from the API key, so a caller cannot
claim to be someone else. `purpose` is mandatory and comes from a fixed list: nobody is
screened without a recorded lawful reason.
Subjects are versioned and immutable. A search pins the exact version it ran against, so a six-month-old result can still say who it was about at the time.

item.name: 3 - Searches
item.description: Start a run. The response is a receipt, not an answer.

request.description:
Returns **202** and a `searchId`. The run is queued; the worker does the work.

A queued run reports `findings: NOT_EVALUATED`. Rendering that would show someone "nothing found" about a search that has not started.

`Idempotency-Key`: send the same value twice and you get **200** with the same id, not a second search.

exec: if (pm.response.code === 200) console.log('Idempotent replay - same key, same search.');

request.description:
THE INTEGRATOR PATH. One call: send the name, get a screening.

subjectRef and subjectSnapshot are mutually exclusive - send exactly one. With subjectSnapshot the service creates the versioned subject and queues the search in the same request, so a tenant that just wants "screen this name" does not have to make two calls.

Use subjectRef instead when you already hold a subjectId and want repeat screenings pinned to the same identity snapshot.

Still 202. The work is queued either way - poll the status URL.

Run until `execution` is `SUCCEEDED`, `PARTIAL`, `FAILED` or `CANCELLED`.

In a Collection Run this re-runs itself until the run settles. `ETag` carries the revision.

exec: // Wait before polling. Without this the 30 attempts complete in milliseconds and the run
// reports "still QUEUED" while the worker is simply still working.
// A busy wait, deliberately: the sandbox does not reliably hold a run open for setTimeout.
pm.test('terminal', () => pm.expect.fail('Still ' + b.execution + ' after 30 polls. Is the worker running? pnpm dev:worker'));

request.description: Scoped to the calling key's tenant. There is no way to ask for another tenant's.
Only while it is still running. A finished search stays finished - cancelling is not a way to erase a result.

item.name: 4 - Results
item.description: What the search produced, and what it could not reach.

request.description:
There is deliberately **no endpoint that returns findings alone**.

- `findings` - each with its band, four axis values and rationale
- `coverage` - whether everything promised was searched
- `sourceOutcomes` - **the FR-05 ladder**: what each rung did, including the rungs nothing is approved for
- `rejectedLeads` - candidates deliberately not promoted, with reasons. Diligence, not noise
- `noMatchStatement` - what an absence does and does not mean
- `mode` - `MOCK` or `LIVE`

A `band` is not a score. Do not rank, average or threshold it into a number.

exec: console.log('mode:', b.mode, '| findings:', b.findings.length, '| rejected:', b.rejectedLeads.length);
console.log('NOT a clean result: nothing found AND not everything searched.');
if (b.mode === 'MOCK') console.log('Fixture data. Nothing was fetched from any real source.');

request.description: The company graph, frozen to this run. An officer who resolved only partially attaches **no** companies - a partial identity match is not an association.

item.name: 5 - Admin: source registry
item.description:
The four-eyes lifecycle. Needs `source_admin`:

```
pnpm key:issue --role source_admin --label "postman admin"
```

`collection` is one of `sources`, `taxonomy`, `policies`.

**Approve needs a different person from the proposer.** With one key, Approve returns 403 - that is the check working. Issue a second key to complete the flow.

request.description: Every source version and its lifecycle state. A source is usable only when a version is ACTIVE.
One version, with its content, rights policy, data profile and history.

**Step 1 of taking the SEC source live.**

The body is exactly what `apps/api/src/sources/registry/sec-litigation-releases.ts` holds, so what you propose here is what is written down and reviewable in the repo.

Note `robotsPosition: NOT_ESTABLISHED` - deliberate. Nobody has read their robots.txt, and the fetch gate refuses that value. Run `pnpm first-contact` before changing it, and change it through this lifecycle rather than by hand.

The same lifecycle, different records. `taxonomy` needs `taxonomy_admin`; `policies` needs `source_admin`.

Activating a taxonomy version runs the **lexicon audit** - it fails activation if any query term maps to a protected characteristic, not only CI.

item.name: 8 - Admin: source health and the kill switch
item.description: What an operator watches once anything is live.

request.description:
Breaker state, budget spend, licence clock and kill switch, per source.

Authenticates with {{operatorKey}}, not the collection-level {{apiKey}}. Source health needs platform:read_health, which platform_operator holds and an analyst key does not — so with the default key this returns 403 while asserting 200. Mint one with: pnpm key:issue --role platform_operator

exec: // Source health needs `platform:read_health`, which `platform_operator` holds and
// `source_admin` does NOT (T06: an operator sees breaker and budget state without being
// handed evidence access). Assert the status before reading the body — a 403 here used to
// crash this script on `rows.forEach`, which hid the refusal instead of reporting it.
'403 means this key lacks platform:read_health — pnpm key:issue --role platform_operator'

item.name: SEC source health - breaker, budget and the last success

request.description:
The same route as above, with the assertions that matter for the SEC specifically. This is the first thing to look at when a live search comes back PARTIAL / UNRESOLVED with a lead rejected at stage FETCH.

breaker OPEN is OUR record of the source refusing us. It is NOT the SEC refusing us right now, and clearing it changes nothing at sec.gov — the only way to find out is the next request. Locally:
    pnpm source:health sec-litigation-releases
    pnpm source:health sec-litigation-releases --reset --reason "why"

The reset clears the recorded breaker, failure counts and budget windows. It does NOT weaken the breaker: the next failure opens it again on the same terms, including the D17 stop conditions. It refuses outside a local stack and refuses to go around a kill switch.

pm.test('a spent budget is visible as a number, not inferred from a failure', () => pm.expect(sec.daily).to.have.property('spent'));

item.name: 9 - Reserved (501 by design)
item.description:
The commercial self-service layer, deferred by **D-007**. These return **501 with a documented reason** rather than 404, so the gap is visible to an integrator instead of looking like something to work around.

Keys are provider-managed this phase: `pnpm key:issue`.

request.description: Plan management is deferred (D-007).
Usage metering is deferred. Counters are recorded but not exposed or billed.
Tenant usage reporting is deferred.

item.name: 10 - Refusals worth seeing
item.description: The API refusing things correctly is most of what it does. Worth running once so the behaviour is familiar before it happens in anger.

request.description: An unauthenticated request gets 401 with no detail about what exists.
The service will not hold a person's name without a recorded reason for screening them.
Schemas are strict. A typo is rejected rather than silently dropped, so a client mistake fails loudly instead of quietly narrowing a search.
FR-05: "EU", "LATAM" and "GLOBAL" are **not** source permissions. Naming one is rejected explicitly rather than silently widening a search's scope.
A tenant learns nothing about what exists outside its own scope - 404, not 403.
Run this with an `analyst` key. Permission is checked per route, not per prefix.

exec: console.log('403 here means your key lacks source_admin. That is the guard working.');

item.name: 11 - SEC go-live (four eyes)
item.description:
Taking the SEC litigation-releases feed live, in the order it must happen.

READ FIRST. Two of these steps are not developer actions:

  * `pnpm first-contact --yes-contact-the-sec` runs OUTSIDE Postman, and the project owner
    runs it. It is the first live request this service makes. DONE 2026-09-16, verdict
    ALLOWED, recorded in docs/sources/sec-robots-evidence.json.
  * APPROVE must be sent with a DIFFERENT key from the one that proposed, by a DIFFERENT
    person. The service compares credentials; it cannot tell humans apart, so the second
    person is real only if they hold {{approverKey}} themselves.

Version 5 is the one to approve: it carries robotsPosition HONOURED taken from the live
robots read. Versions 1-4 are stale drafts from collection test runs and must NOT be
approved.

request.description: Confirm what you are about to approve. Check two things: `robotsPosition` is HONOURED, and `proposedBy` is NOT the key you are about to approve with.

exec: pm.test('robots position recorded from the live read', () =>
// The revision is the concurrency token the next request must send.
pm.test("not already active", () => pm.expect(b.status, "This local DB already has v" + b.version + " at " + b.status).to.not.eql("ACTIVE"));

item.name: 2. APPROVE - four eyes, second person, reason required

request.description:
The approval. Sent with {{approverKey}}, which must be held by someone other than the proposer.

PUT A REAL NAME IN THE REASON. The audit trail stores the KEY id, not a person, so the reason text is the only place a future reader learns who decided and why. It is mandatory and the service rejects an empty one.

exec: throw new Error("Set approverName and approverRole to the real second person before approving.");
throw new Error("No approverKey set. Paste the second source_admin key into approverKey.");
throw new Error("apiKey and approverKey are the same secret; four-eyes approval needs a different key holder.");
console.log('The approver key is the same identity as the proposer. Use a different key.');

request.description: Not four eyes. This is the rights clearance: nothing reaches ACTIVE without a passing clearance to point at. A refusal here leaves the version at APPROVED with the clearance attached saying why — so "why is this source not live?" always has an answer.
The source is ACTIVE and the fetch gate will now permit it. Until this reads ACTIVE, a live search will refuse the source and report a coverage gap rather than searching it.

item.name: 12 - Tenant: your own API keys
item.description:
Every request here authenticates with {{adminKey}}, NOT the collection-level {{apiKey}}.

These routes need apikey:manage, which tenant_admin holds and analyst does not. The {{apiKey}} in the shipped environments is an ANALYST key, so inheriting it returned 403 on every request while the assertions expected 201/200 - a credential mismatch in the environment, not a fault in the API.

If {{adminKey}} is empty in your environment, mint one:
    pnpm key:issue --tenant tenant-alpha --env sandbox --role tenant_admin --role analyst --label "postman"
Or run folder 13 first and use {{issuedKey}}: signup grants the first user both tenant_admin and analyst.

---

Self-service key management (decision D-050, replacing the D-007 deferral). A tenant issues,
lists and revokes its own machine keys — no operator involved.

Needs the `apikey:manage` permission, which `tenant_admin` holds. Set {{apiKey}} to a
tenant_admin key first:

    pnpm key:issue --role tenant_admin --label "your name"

THE SECRET COMES BACK ONCE. Only a hash is stored, so no endpoint can return it again and
no support process can recover it. The first request below saves it into {{issuedKey}} so
you can use it immediately, but it is gone from the server the moment the response is sent.

Three things self-service deliberately is not, each with a request here that proves it:
  * a path to roles you do not already hold
  * a way across a tenant boundary
  * a way to buy live access — entitlement is sold by the provider, not granted by a key

request.description:
Roles must be ones you already hold. Omit `scopes` to get the scopes those roles can use — an explicit list can only narrow, never widen.

`expiresInDays` may be null for a key that never expires, which is a choice rather than a default.

exec: pm.test('the secret is returned, once', () => pm.expect(b.secret).to.be.a('string'));

request.description:
Every key this tenant holds. Carries no secret and no hash of one — the listing is not a slower way of handing the secret back.

`status` is derived at read time, so a key whose expiry passed while nothing was running still reads EXPIRED.

exec: // The property worth asserting every time: no secret ever appears here.

request.description:
Worth running once. Without this rule the weakest tenant_admin credential mints a platform_admin one and the role model is decoration.

The refusal names the specific role you were missing, because "forbidden" on its own sends an integrator back to re-read the role table.

item.name: 4. A live key from a sandbox credential is refused

request.description:
Run this with a SANDBOX {{apiKey}}. Two independent conditions gate a live key: your tenant must be entitled to live, and your own credential must be live.

Entitlement is a commercial act by the provider. Self-service issues credentials within what was sold; it does not sell.

exec: console.log('You are using a LIVE credential on an entitled tenant, so this succeeded.');

item.name: 5. Pause it - reversible, and not the same as revoking

request.description:
The key stops authenticating immediately - and `enable` brings it back with the same secret and the same key id, so nothing in your configuration changes.

**Not for a leaked secret.** Anything reversible is the wrong answer to a credential somebody else now holds; use `DELETE`, which is permanent. This is for a paused integration, a rotation window, or a key you want out of service while a question is answered.

List your keys after this and the entry reads `status: "DISABLED"` with the reason you gave. A revoked key answers 409 here rather than pretending to pause.

exec: pm.test('and it is the reversible field', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().disabled).to.eql(true));

request.description:
The same secret works again the moment this returns. Nothing is re-issued.

A **revoked** key answers 409 instead: `revokedAt` is one-way and this route cannot touch it. That is the whole distinction between the two - both stop the key, and only one of them can be undone.

Immediate and irreversible. The reason is mandatory and is written to the audit trail.

A key belonging to another tenant answers 404, not 403 — the second would confirm that it exists.

item.name: 13 - Tenant E2E: signup to adverse search
item.description:
SIGNUP IS RATE LIMITED: 5 per origin per hour (D-056). Run this folder a sixth time within the hour and 13.1/14.1 returns 429 and the folder halts. That is the limiter working, not a broken signup. Either wait, or clear the bucket on a local stack:

    mongosh "$MONGODB_URI" --eval 'db.attemptLog.deleteMany({bucket:"SIGNUP"})'

THE WHOLE FLOW, RUNNABLE WITH "RUN FOLDER" AND NOTHING ELSE.

A stranger signs up, confirms an address, signs in, issues its own sandbox AND live keys, and uses the sandbox one to run an adverse-media search to a terminal result. No Mongo shell, no seeded credential, no editing variables between requests.

Every request from 13.7 onward OVERRIDES the collection-level auth and sends `Authorization: ApiKey {{issuedKey}}` - the key the tenant minted for itself at 13.5. That is the point of the folder: proving a brand-new tenant consumes the API exactly as an external customer would, not as the seeded tenant-alpha.

Each request stops the run on an unexpected response rather than cascading failures.

Requires the local stack: pnpm local:up && pnpm local:bootstrap

request.description:
No credential: signup has to work for somebody who does not have one yet.

The address is a fresh {{$guid}} every run, so the folder is re-runnable without hitting D-057's 409 for an address already registered.

Writes tenant, entitlement, taxonomy, policy AND the administrator in ONE transaction. The administrator is granted tenant_admin AND analyst: the first carries apikey:manage so they can issue a key, the second carries search:create and is the only role mapped to the search:write scope. Without both, the key issued at 13.5 could not run a search.

exec: pm.test('the tenant id was generated, not chosen', () => pm.expect(b.tenantId).to.match(/^tenant-[0-9a-f-]{36}$/));
pm.test('live still waits for a confirmed address (D-052)', () => pm.expect(b.liveAccess.granted).to.eql(false));

request.description:
DEVELOPMENT ONLY, AND ABSENT IN PRODUCTION.

No mail transport is configured (D-058): the local stack writes every message to an outboundEmails collection, and that collection IS the inbox. This route reads the latest message for ONE named address and returns the token, so the flow no longer leaves Postman for a Mongo shell.

It is not registered at all when NODE_ENV=production — the path does not exist there, rather than existing behind a check somebody could inverit. `email` is required, so this is never a listing of who the customers are.

It only reads. The token it shows is the same single-use, expiring token the email carries; 13.3 still spends it.

exec: pm.test('a token was parsed out of the body', () => pm.expect(b.token).to.be.a('string'));

request.description:
THIS IS THE CALL THAT UNLOCKS A LIVE KEY (D-052).

It sets emailVerifiedAt on the tenant, which is the value key issuance reads — so liveAccessUnlocked here is the same answer POST /v1/tenant/api-keys will now give.

The token works once. Sending it again is refused.
